title: Immunology Foundations, Antigens, Cells and Cytokines — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Immunology lectures (S. A. Sakyi): introduction, antigens, immune cells and cytokines

questions.stem: What characteristic most clearly distinguishes adaptive from innate immune responses?
questions.why: Adaptive responses expand lymphocyte clones with receptors specific for the encountered antigen. Some cells persist as memory cells and respond more rapidly to the same antigen on re-exposure.

notes.A: Physical barriers are pre-existing innate defences that can act without a prior encounter.
notes.C: Germline-encoded receptors recognise broad motifs in innate immunity. Adaptive antigen receptors acquire much of their diversity by gene rearrangement.
notes.D: B and T lymphocytes are central to adaptive immunity and generate its antigen-specific responses.
notes.E: Constitutively expressed antimicrobial peptides are part of first-line innate defence.

questions.stem: Which type of immunity follows an individual's own response to vaccination?
questions.why: Vaccination deliberately exposes an individual to antigen or instructions for an antigen. The recipient's own lymphocytes respond and can form memory, so the immunity is artificial and active.

notes.A: Artificial passive immunity involves deliberate administration of preformed antibodies rather than induction of the recipient's response.
notes.B: Natural passive immunity arises when antibodies are transferred naturally, for example across the placenta.
notes.C: Innate defences may help initiate a vaccine response, but antigen-specific memory is adaptive.
notes.E: Maternal antibody transfer supplies preformed antibody without generating the recipient's own vaccine response.

questions.stem: A newborn receives protective IgG from the mother without producing it. Which type of immunity is illustrated?
questions.why: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and can protect the newborn temporarily. The transfer is natural, and the immunity is passive because the infant receives finished antibodies.

notes.B: Natural active immunity involves making one's own response following a naturally occurring exposure.
notes.C: Artificial active immunity follows deliberate immunisation that stimulates the recipient's own lymphocytes.
notes.D: Innate cellular immunity uses cells such as phagocytes and does not describe transfer of maternal IgG.
notes.E: Vaccine-induced memory requires active priming of the recipient's lymphocytes.

questions.stem: Which defence is part of the body's immediate anatomical barrier system?
questions.why: Airway mucus traps inhaled material and coordinated beating of cilia moves it towards the pharynx for removal. This mechanical barrier works without antigen-specific priming.

notes.A: Class-switched IgG memory is generated by adaptive lymphocyte responses after antigen exposure.
notes.B: Germinal-centre selection is an adaptive process that favours antigen-responsive B-cell clones.
notes.D: Clonal expansion of CD8 cells is a later, antigen-specific adaptive response.
notes.E: Long-lived plasma cells produce antibodies after adaptive differentiation, rather than contributing to a mechanical barrier.

questions.stem: Which antimicrobial constituent of tears hydrolyses bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan?
questions.why: Lysozyme in tears hydrolyses a glycosidic bond in bacterial peptidoglycan. Weakening that structural polymer contributes to chemical protection of the eye surface.

notes.A: Elastase is a protease and does not cleave the carbohydrate backbone of peptidoglycan.
notes.B: Catalase decomposes hydrogen peroxide rather than digesting peptidoglycan in tears.
notes.C: Trypsin is a digestive protease that cleaves peptide bonds and is not the tear enzyme asked about.
notes.D: Amylase hydrolyses starch-related carbohydrates rather than the linked sugars of peptidoglycan.

questions.stem: Who is classically associated with demonstrating phagocytosis as a cellular mechanism of immunity?
questions.why: Metchnikoff described cells engulfing foreign material and argued that phagocytosis defends the host. His work helped establish a cellular basis for innate immunity.

notes.A: Jenner developed protective smallpox vaccination using cowpox, rather than establishing the role of phagocytes.
notes.C: Landsteiner is known for identifying major human blood groups and studying antigen specificity.
notes.D: Ehrlich contributed to theories of antibody formation and humoral immunity.
notes.E: Koch helped establish the microbial causes of diseases through bacteriological work.

questions.stem: Which researcher is linked most directly to the original protective smallpox vaccination work?
questions.why: Edward Jenner showed that inoculation with cowpox could protect against smallpox. His observations became the basis for subsequent smallpox vaccination.

notes.A: Pasteur developed later vaccines, including one against rabies, rather than originating Jenner's smallpox vaccination work.
notes.B: Ehrlich helped develop concepts of antibody formation and mechanisms of immunity.
notes.C: Koch is associated with identifying pathogenic bacteria and establishing their role in disease.
notes.E: Metchnikoff is known for investigating phagocytosis rather than founding smallpox vaccination.

questions.stem: Which response often occurs within minutes of a novel microbial encounter rather than requiring clonal expansion?
questions.why: Resident innate cells already express pattern-recognition receptors. On detecting microbial material, they can rapidly release inflammatory mediators without waiting for antigen-specific clones to proliferate.

notes.B: Affinity maturation involves mutation and selection among activated B-cell clones over time.
notes.C: Memory B-cell differentiation requires prior adaptive activation and does not explain the earliest response to a novel antigen.
notes.D: A secondary IgG response involves previous adaptive priming rather than a first innate encounter.
notes.E: Naive T-cell effector expansion requires antigen presentation, activation and cell division.

questions.stem: What do pattern-recognition receptors chiefly detect on microorganisms?
questions.why: Pattern-recognition receptors recognise recurring microbial features such as bacterial cell-wall products. Detection of these shared motifs can trigger antimicrobial and inflammatory responses.

notes.A: Antibody variable regions are products of adaptive lymphocytes rather than recurring microbial motifs.
notes.B: T-cell receptor clonotypes are generated by somatic rearrangement in lymphocytes and are not the microbial targets of these receptors.
notes.D: HLA haplotypes specify host antigen-presenting molecules and do not describe conserved microbial patterns.
notes.E: Mature B-cell antibodies recognise specific antigenic structures and are not the general targets detected by pattern-recognition receptors.

questions.stem: Which receptor recognizes bacterial lipopolysaccharide with accessory components?
questions.why: Bacterial lipopolysaccharide is recognised by a complex involving TLR4 and MD-2. CD14 helps deliver the ligand, allowing activation of innate signalling.

notes.A: TLR3 is best known for recognising double-stranded RNA rather than bacterial lipopolysaccharide.
notes.B: CD19 is a B-cell co-receptor involved in amplifying antigen-receptor signals.
notes.C: CD3 is the signalling complex associated with the T-cell antigen receptor.
notes.D: The high-affinity Fc epsilon receptor is an IgE receptor, not the receptor that recognises lipopolysaccharide.

questions.stem: A macrophage binds a conserved microbial pattern via a Toll-like receptor. Which response is expected?
questions.why: Toll-like receptor activation in macrophages initiates signalling that can increase expression of inflammatory cytokines. These mediators recruit or activate other cells of the innate response.

notes.A: Immunoglobulin class switching occurs in B cells and is not an immediate macrophage response.
notes.C: The engaged receptor is on the macrophage, so its signal does not make the bacterium divide.
notes.D: Antibody affinity maturation requires selection among activated B-cell clones rather than macrophage signalling alone.
notes.E: Immunoglobulin gene rearrangement is a developmental process in B cells rather than a Toll-like receptor output in macrophages.

questions.stem: What does an opsonin chiefly do in host defence?

options.label: B
options.text: Convert memory B cells into platelets

questions.why: Opsonins such as IgG and C3b coat a target and provide ligands for receptors on phagocytes. This improves attachment and enables more efficient engulfment.

notes.A: Opsonisation promotes recognition of the target and does not require blocking cytokine receptors.
notes.B: B cells and platelets are separate lineages, and target coating does not convert one into the other.
notes.C: C3b can promote opsonisation, whereas the terminal complement complex forms pores in suitable target membranes.
notes.E: Neutrophils can still migrate in response to chemotactic signals and use opsonins when they reach a target.

questions.stem: Which macrophage process illustrates oxygen-dependent microbial killing?
questions.why: Phagocyte NADPH oxidase uses oxygen to produce superoxide during the respiratory burst. Superoxide and its reactive derivatives help kill engulfed microbes.

notes.B: Lysozyme hydrolyses peptidoglycan and can act independently of a respiratory burst.
notes.C: Defensins can damage microbial membranes without relying on oxidant generation.
notes.D: Membrane fusion delivers lysosomal contents to the phagosome but does not itself generate reactive oxygen species.
notes.E: Antigen presentation displays peptides to lymphocytes rather than illustrating oxidant-mediated microbial killing.

questions.stem: Which antimicrobial molecule contributes to oxygen-independent killing in phagolysosomes?
questions.why: Lysozyme damages susceptible bacterial cell walls by cleaving bonds in peptidoglycan. Its hydrolytic action does not depend on production of reactive oxygen species.

notes.A: Superoxide is a reactive oxygen species formed when NADPH oxidase reduces molecular oxygen.
notes.B: Hydrogen peroxide is an oxygen-derived oxidant involved in antimicrobial killing.
notes.D: Myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide and chloride to make hypochlorous acid, an oxidative antimicrobial.
notes.E: Nitric oxide synthesis by nitric oxide synthase uses molecular oxygen and yields a reactive nitrogen species.

questions.stem: Which substance can specifically bind immune receptors but cannot alone induce a robust immune response?
questions.why: A hapten can bind specifically to an antibody or B-cell receptor but is generally insufficient to induce an immune response by itself. A linked immunogenic carrier can provide T-cell help.

notes.A: An immunogen is capable of eliciting an immune response under suitable conditions.
notes.B: A superantigen can trigger activation of many T cells by linking MHC class II molecules to certain T-cell receptor regions.
notes.C: A toxoid is an inactivated toxin that can act as an immunogen while retaining relevant antigenic structures.
notes.D: A live vaccine is designed to elicit an active host response rather than acting only as a small binding determinant.

questions.stem: What is the smallest antigenic site recognized by an antibody or T-cell receptor called?
questions.why: An epitope is the part of an antigen that is specifically recognised. An antibody binds it directly, whereas a conventional T-cell receptor recognises a processed peptide in the context of MHC.

notes.A: A paratope is the antibody combining surface that binds the epitope.
notes.C: An isotype is a class of immunoglobulin defined by constant-region features.
notes.D: An allotype is an inherited allelic variant of an immunoglobulin or another protein, rather than a general term for an antigenic site.
notes.E: A haplotype is a set of linked genetic variants inherited together.

questions.stem: Which antibody region directly interacts with an epitope on an antigen?
questions.why: The paratope is the antigen-binding surface made primarily by variable loops from the heavy and light chains. Its shape and chemistry determine which epitope the antibody binds.

notes.A: The Fc region mediates effector functions, such as interactions with Fc receptors.
notes.B: The J chain helps assemble polymeric immunoglobulins, including IgM and secretory IgA.
notes.C: Hinge disulphides help join antibody heavy chains but do not form the antigen-combining surface.
notes.E: The gamma constant region determines IgG class and effector features rather than the primary binding specificity.

questions.stem: Which epitope depends on residues that are distant in sequence but adjacent in a folded protein?
questions.why: Protein folding can place residues far apart in the sequence next to one another on its surface. A conformational epitope depends on that three-dimensional arrangement.

notes.B: A linear epitope is formed from a continuous stretch of amino acids.
notes.C: A stop codon signals the end of translation and is not itself a residue in the folded antigen.
notes.D: A signal peptide directs protein targeting and does not define an epitope assembled from distant residues.
notes.E: An intron is a nucleic acid segment removed during RNA processing, not a surface of the folded protein.

questions.stem: Which antigen-processing route typically presents extracellularly acquired protein antigens to CD4-positive helper T cells?
questions.why: Antigen-presenting cells can degrade endocytosed proteins in acidic vesicles. The resulting peptides bind MHC class II molecules for recognition by CD4-positive T cells.

notes.A: MHC class I is the main pathway for presenting peptides from cytosolic proteins to CD8-positive T cells.
notes.B: CD1 molecules present lipid antigens rather than handling the conventional peptide pathway to CD4 helper cells.
notes.D: Fc receptors can help internalise some antigens but their recycling does not display processed peptides.
notes.E: C9 polymerisation forms part of terminal complement attack and does not present peptides to T cells.

questions.stem: Which pathway predominantly displays peptides from viral proteins synthesized inside an infected host cell?
questions.why: Proteins made inside an infected cell can be degraded to peptides in the cytosol. Loading peptides onto MHC class I allows CD8-positive T cells to survey the cell.

notes.A: MHC class II usually presents peptides derived from material processed in endosomal compartments to CD4 T cells.
notes.B: Secretory IgA transport delivers antibody across epithelium and does not display intracellular peptides.
notes.C: Alternative complement activation is an extracellular mechanism for marking susceptible surfaces.
notes.D: Mast-cell Fc epsilon receptor signalling is triggered by IgE engagement, rather than displaying peptides to CD8 cells.

questions.stem: What term describes an antigenic difference between individuals of the same species, as with ABO groups?
questions.why: An alloantigen differs among individuals of one species because of inherited variation. ABO blood-group determinants can therefore be recognised as foreign when cells are transferred between incompatible individuals.

notes.A: A xenoantigen originates from a different species rather than another individual of the same species.
notes.C: An autoantigen is a host's own antigen recognised by that host's immune system.
notes.D: Heterophile antigens are antigenically related structures that can occur in different species and cross-react.
notes.E: A tumour-associated antigen is associated with malignant cells and is not the general term for inherited ABO variation.

questions.stem: What term applies to an antigen derived from a different species?
questions.why: A xenoantigen is an antigen from another species. Such a determinant may be recognised as foreign after transfer of cells or tissue across species.

notes.A: An alloantigen is a variable antigen found among individuals within the same species.
notes.B: An autoantigen is a component of the responding host's own body.
notes.C: A self determinant is a recognisable structure that belongs to the host rather than another species.
notes.E: Idiotype determinants are features of the variable region of an antibody or antigen receptor.

questions.stem: Why can antibodies against one microorganism react with a distinct organism?

options.label: A
options.text: They recognize shared or similar epitopes

options.label: B
options.text: They convert one bacterial species into another

questions.why: An antibody binds a local shape and chemical pattern. If a different organism carries a sufficiently similar epitope, that antibody may bind it as well.

notes.B: Antibody binding can neutralise or label microbes, but it does not change a microbe's species.
notes.C: Antibodies bind antigen through their variable regions. General cleavage of immunoglobulins does not explain cross-reactivity.
notes.D: A shared epitope can occur even when the organisms' genomes are different.
notes.E: Cross-reacting antibodies can bind shared protein or carbohydrate determinants without recognising microbial DNA.

questions.stem: Which antigen type usually requires helper T-cell cooperation for high-affinity class-switched antibody responses?
questions.why: B cells that bind a protein can present derived peptides to helper T cells on MHC class II. The resulting help promotes germinal-centre selection and class switching.

notes.A: Repetitive polysaccharides can activate B cells without classical cognate T-cell help, typically with limited affinity maturation.
notes.B: Uncoupled haptens can bind receptors but generally lack linked helper peptides needed for a strong response.
notes.D: Some lipids can be presented by CD1, but isolated self lipids do not exemplify the conventional protein-dependent antibody response.
notes.E: Inert glass supplies no protein peptide for presentation to a cognate helper T cell.

questions.stem: Which response is typically associated with a T-independent repetitive polysaccharide antigen?

options.label: D
options.text: Dependence on MHC class II peptides

questions.why: Repeated polysaccharide structures can cross-link many B-cell receptors without conventional peptide-specific T-cell help. Such responses are typically dominated by IgM, although some class switching can occur.

notes.A: Strong germinal-centre affinity maturation usually requires signals from cognate T follicular helper cells.
notes.B: Some class switching can occur, but a dominant and sustained switched response is less typical without T-cell help.
notes.C: Cytotoxic T cells kill selected targets and do not define this type of B-cell response to polysaccharide.
notes.D: These antigens do not need to supply a carrier peptide for classical MHC class II-dependent T-cell help.

questions.stem: Why does coupling a small hapten to a carrier protein increase immunogenicity?

options.label: D
options.text: It destroys the hapten's chemical group

options.label: E
options.text: It excludes processing by antigen-presenting cells

questions.why: A hapten-specific B cell binds and internalises the conjugate, then presents peptides from the linked carrier. Carrier-specific helper T cells can then provide signals that activate the B cell.

notes.A: Hapten recognition is retained, allowing a hapten-specific B cell to take up the linked carrier.
notes.C: Binding by the B-cell receptor is the first step in internalising the conjugate.
notes.D: The relevant effect is addition of linked peptide determinants through a carrier, rather than loss of the hapten epitope.
notes.E: Internalisation allows the B cell to process carrier peptides and present them to helper cells.

questions.stem: Which preparation distinguishes complete from incomplete Freund's adjuvant?

options.label: B
options.text: A preparation rich in IgM antibodies

questions.why: Complete Freund's adjuvant contains killed mycobacterial material that is absent from the incomplete form. That material supplies additional innate immune stimulation.

notes.A: Lysozyme is an antimicrobial enzyme and is not the defining component added to complete Freund's adjuvant.
notes.B: IgM is an immunoglobulin class rather than the component distinguishing these two adjuvants.
notes.C: Albumin can be used as an antigen or carrier protein but does not define the complete adjuvant.
notes.E: Antithrombin regulates coagulation proteases and is not the immune stimulant distinguishing the two preparations.

questions.stem: What is the intended immunological function of a vaccine adjuvant?

options.label: A
options.text: Enhance the immune response to antigen

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce cytokine signalling from helper T cells

questions.why: An adjuvant helps an antigen induce a stronger or more suitable immune response. Depending on the formulation, it can improve antigen presentation or stimulate innate signals that support lymphocyte activation.

notes.B: Dendritic-cell activation can improve antigen presentation and support the vaccine response, rather than being universally blocked.
notes.C: An adjuvant should preserve useful antigenic structures so that the immune response can recognise them.
notes.D: Helper T-cell cytokines can support adaptive immunity, and suppression of those signals is not the aim here.
notes.E: Clonal expansion of antigen-specific lymphocytes is an expected part of an effective vaccine response.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a bacterial superantigen from a conventional peptide antigen?

options.label: A
options.text: It is presented only by red blood cells

options.label: B
options.text: It binds only rearranged B-cell receptors

options.label: C
options.text: It activates many T-cell clones at once

options.label: E
options.text: It lacks any capacity to bind MHC molecules

questions.why: A bacterial superantigen can bridge MHC class II and a variable region of the T-cell receptor outside the normal peptide-recognition site. This activates many clones sharing that receptor feature.

notes.A: Mature red cells do not express MHC class II, whereas professional presenting cells can participate in superantigen signalling.
notes.B: A classical bacterial superantigen engages T-cell receptors and MHC class II rather than only binding B-cell receptors.
notes.D: Broad activation does not require conventional processing into a peptide specific to each activated T-cell clone.
notes.E: MHC class II binding is part of the mechanism by which classic bacterial superantigens activate T cells.

questions.stem: Which cell population is commonly first recruited from blood during acute bacterial inflammation?
questions.why: Neutrophils rapidly leave the circulation in response to inflammatory signals and are often the dominant early recruited leukocytes in acute bacterial inflammation. They can phagocytose and kill microbes.

notes.A: Eosinophils are most strongly associated with type 2 immunity and certain parasitic or allergic responses.
notes.B: Naive B cells mainly recirculate through lymphoid organs and require antigen signals to mount adaptive responses.
notes.C: Basophils release mediators in type 2 responses and are not the major early phagocytes in typical bacterial inflammation.
notes.D: Plasma cells secrete antibody after B-cell differentiation rather than being the first recruited phagocytes.

questions.stem: Which cell is especially important for presenting processed antigen to naive T lymphocytes?
questions.why: Activated dendritic cells are especially effective at initiating naive T-cell responses. They display processed peptides on MHC and provide the costimulatory signals needed for priming.

notes.A: Mature erythrocytes transport oxygen and generally do not express the MHC and costimulatory machinery needed for priming.
notes.C: Platelets function principally in haemostasis and are not the main cells that prime naive T lymphocytes.
notes.D: Basophils release inflammatory mediators in type 2 responses and are not the usual professional priming cells for naive T cells.
notes.E: Fibroblasts make extracellular matrix and generally lack the full costimulatory capacity needed to prime naive T cells.

questions.stem: Which leukocyte most directly participates in defence against large helminth parasites?
questions.why: Eosinophils are recruited in type 2 responses to many helminths. They can release granule proteins onto parasite surfaces that are too large to engulf.

notes.A: Neutrophils are prominent phagocytes in acute bacterial and fungal defence, rather than the classic granulocytes of helminth responses.
notes.B: Erythrocytes carry oxygen and do not release antiparasite cytotoxic granules.
notes.C: Platelets contribute to haemostasis but are not leukocytes specialised for this type of parasite-directed degranulation.
notes.E: Reticulocytes are immature red cells, not granule-bearing immune cells.

questions.stem: Which circulating leukocyte can degranulate and release histamine in immediate allergy?
questions.why: Circulating basophils carry high-affinity IgE receptors. Allergen cross-linking of bound IgE can trigger release of preformed histamine.

notes.B: Neutrophils release antimicrobial granule products but are not the conventional circulating source of IgE-triggered histamine.
notes.C: Monocytes are phagocytic precursors of tissue cells and are not the typical immediate histamine-releasing granulocytes.
notes.D: Dendritic cells mainly process and present antigens to T cells, rather than storing histamine for rapid allergic degranulation.
notes.E: Cytotoxic T cells release perforin and granzymes to kill selected targets rather than histamine in immediate allergy.

questions.stem: Where are mast cells typically resident before an allergic response?
questions.why: Mast-cell precursors mature locally and remain in connective tissues and mucosae. Cells near vessels and epithelial surfaces can therefore respond rapidly to local allergens.

notes.A: The erythrocyte fraction contains red cells. Mature mast cells are primarily tissue residents.
notes.B: Mast-cell precursors originate in marrow, but mature mast cells are distinct from the neutrophil reserve.
notes.D: Mast cells are living cells present in tissue rather than soluble components of plasma.
notes.E: The tubular lumen carries filtrate and is not a usual site of mast-cell residence.

questions.stem: Which cell-surface marker is associated with most mature T lymphocytes?
questions.why: CD3 is associated with the surface T-cell receptor on mature T cells. Its signalling chains transmit the signal after the receptor engages its target.

notes.A: CD19 is a common B-lineage marker and part of the B-cell co-receptor complex.
notes.B: CD14 participates in recognition of lipopolysaccharide and is commonly expressed by monocytes.
notes.C: CD56 is often used to identify natural killer cells, typically in combination with absence of CD3.
notes.D: CD41 is part of platelet integrin alpha-IIb beta-3 and is associated with megakaryocytes and platelets.

questions.stem: Which surface marker is especially useful for identifying B lymphocytes?
questions.why: CD19 is expressed across much of B-cell development and on most mature B cells. It is commonly used to label the B-cell lineage by immunophenotyping.

notes.A: CD3 is a component of the T-cell receptor complex and is used to identify T cells.
notes.C: CD14 is commonly used as a monocyte marker and participates in lipopolysaccharide recognition.
notes.D: CD56 is associated with natural killer cells and is not the standard B-lineage marker.
notes.E: CD15 is associated with granulocytes and some other cells rather than being a typical B-cell marker.

questions.stem: Which marker is typical of circulating monocytes and macrophage-lineage cells?
questions.why: CD14 is expressed by many monocytes and macrophage-lineage cells. It helps deliver lipopolysaccharide to the TLR4 signalling complex.

notes.A: CD19 is associated with B lymphocytes, not the usual marker for monocytes.
notes.B: CD3 is a component of the T-cell receptor complex and marks T-lineage cells.
notes.C: CD56 is used particularly in identifying natural killer cells rather than classical monocytes.
notes.E: CD8 is the common co-receptor of cytotoxic T lymphocytes, not the characteristic monocyte marker.

questions.stem: Which combination identifies a conventional helper T lymphocyte?
questions.why: Conventional helper T cells express the CD3 T-cell signalling complex and the CD4 co-receptor. CD4 assists recognition of peptide presented by MHC class II.

notes.B: CD3 with CD8 is typical of conventional cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
notes.C: CD19 and CD20 are used together as markers of mature B cells.
notes.D: CD14 and CD16 can be used to distinguish monocyte subsets and do not indicate conventional helper T cells.
notes.E: CD56 with CD16 is commonly found on circulating natural killer cells.

questions.stem: Which combination is most characteristic of a conventional cytotoxic T lymphocyte?
questions.why: Conventional cytotoxic T lymphocytes carry the CD3 signalling complex and the CD8 co-receptor. CD8 assists recognition of peptide displayed by MHC class I.

notes.A: CD3 and CD4 together are typical of conventional helper T lymphocytes.
notes.B: CD19 and CD21 are B-cell markers, with CD21 also acting as a complement receptor.
notes.D: CD14 and CD16 can characterise monocyte subsets, rather than establishing T-cell lineage.
notes.E: CD56 and CD57 can occur on mature natural killer cells and some T cells, but do not establish the conventional CD8 T-cell phenotype.

questions.stem: Which pair of markers is useful for identifying many circulating natural killer cells?
questions.why: Many circulating natural killer cells are CD56-positive and express CD16, an Fc receptor. In clinical phenotyping they are typically also distinguished from T cells by absence of CD3.

notes.A: CD3 and CD4 are characteristic of helper T lymphocytes rather than natural killer cells.
notes.B: CD19 and CD20 are characteristic B-cell markers rather than the typical NK-cell markers.
notes.C: CD14 with CD11b is a common myeloid phenotype and is not the usual NK-cell marker combination.
notes.D: CD41 and CD61 are subunits of a platelet integrin and mark platelets or megakaryocytes.

questions.stem: Why can an NK cell kill a virally infected cell showing reduced MHC class I expression?

options.label: A
options.text: Excessive stimulation of B-cell class switching

options.label: C
options.text: Direct recognition of an HLA-II peptide via TCR

options.label: D
options.text: Conversion of target cell MHC I into IgG

options.label: E
options.text: Release of extracellular antibodies by NK cells

questions.why: Self MHC class I normally engages inhibitory receptors on NK cells. Reduced class I weakens that inhibition, so activating inputs can dominate and trigger killing.

notes.A: B-cell class switching changes the antibody constant region and does not account for NK-cell detection of reduced MHC class I.
notes.C: NK cells lack the conventional rearranged T-cell receptor used for peptide–MHC recognition.
notes.D: MHC class I and IgG are distinct proteins. A fall in class I changes an inhibitory signal.
notes.E: NK cells are cytotoxic lymphocytes and do not secrete antibodies to provide this recognition.

questions.stem: Which mechanism allows NK cells to kill antibody-coated targets?
questions.why: In antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, CD16 on an NK cell binds the Fc region of IgG already attached to a target. That recognition can trigger release of cytotoxic granules.

notes.A: The classical complement pathway uses C1q to initiate a separate extracellular mechanism of antibody-dependent defence.
notes.B: Affinity maturation improves antibody binding during B-cell selection and does not cause NK-cell degranulation directly.
notes.C: Class switching changes antibody isotype during a B-cell response rather than describing NK-cell killing.
notes.E: B-cell receptor recombination generates receptor diversity before antigen-driven responses.

questions.stem: Which cytotoxic proteins are central to the common NK-cell granule killing pathway?
questions.why: Natural killer cells release perforin and granzymes at contacts with targets. Perforin enables granzymes to reach the target-cell cytosol, where they can trigger apoptosis.

notes.B: Albumin and transferrin are plasma carrier proteins, not a cytotoxic granule pair.
notes.C: Fibrin is structural material in a clot, while prothrombin is a precursor of a clotting enzyme.
notes.D: Lysozyme and amylase are hydrolytic enzymes, but do not constitute the standard NK-cell apoptotic pathway.
notes.E: Histones and nucleosomes package DNA rather than delivering the cytotoxic signal from NK granules.

questions.stem: How do macrophages efficiently engulf IgG-coated organisms?
questions.why: Fc gamma receptors on macrophages bind the exposed Fc domains of IgG coating a target. Receptor clustering triggers signalling and cytoskeletal changes needed for phagocytosis.

notes.A: Nuclear steroid receptors regulate gene expression and do not recognise target-bound immunoglobulin at the cell surface.
notes.B: cGMP-gated channels respond to a cyclic nucleotide rather than binding the Fc portion of IgG.
notes.D: Plasminogen receptors support local proteolysis, but macrophage recognition of IgG requires Fc-binding receptors.
notes.E: Haemoglobin binds oxygen within red cells and does not mediate IgG-directed target recognition by macrophages.

questions.stem: Which feature describes cytokine pleiotropy?

options.label: A
options.text: Many cytokines yield one fixed effect

options.label: D
options.text: Cytokines are stored in secretory granules

questions.why: Pleiotropy means that a single cytokine can have multiple effects. Its action may differ between responding cells because they express different receptors or signalling programmes.

notes.A: Many cytokines sharing an effect is redundancy rather than pleiotropy.
notes.B: Cytokines that oppose one another illustrate antagonism, even if they act on the same cell.
notes.C: Cytokine effects require responsive cells with suitable receptors. Receptor independence is not a feature of pleiotropy.
notes.D: How a cytokine is stored does not define the number of effects it can produce.

questions.stem: What does cytokine redundancy mean?

options.label: C
options.text: A cytokine binds a non-immune cell

options.label: E
options.text: A cytokine is cleaved into many parts

questions.why: Cytokine redundancy means that more than one cytokine can produce a similar outcome. Distinct receptors may converge on shared signalling pathways or target functions.

notes.A: One protein recognising several epitopes does not describe overlapping functions of several cytokines.
notes.C: Activity on a non-immune cell can illustrate pleiotropy but does not establish a shared effect between different cytokines.
notes.D: Inhibition between cytokines is antagonism rather than redundancy.
notes.E: Protein cleavage is a processing event and does not define shared biological effects across several mediators.

questions.stem: Which intracellular pathway transmits signals from many class I cytokine receptors?
questions.why: Many class I cytokine receptors associate with Janus kinases rather than having intrinsic kinase domains. Ligand binding activates JAKs, leading to STAT phosphorylation and changes in transcription.

notes.A: Calmodulin is a calcium sensor and is not the principal transcriptional relay for this receptor class.
notes.B: Transducin is a G protein of the retinal light-response pathway.
notes.C: Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin in coagulation rather than conveying a cytokine signal to the nucleus.
notes.E: Adenosine degradation forms purine breakdown products and does not transmit a cytokine receptor signal.

questions.stem: Which cytokine is a key inducer of Th1 differentiation?
questions.why: Antigen-presenting cells can produce IL-12, which promotes the Th1 differentiation programme and interferon-gamma production. This response helps the host control many intracellular microbes.

notes.B: IL-4 is a characteristic polarising signal for Th2 rather than Th1 differentiation.
notes.C: IL-5 supports eosinophil development and activation rather than being a main Th1-inducing cytokine.
notes.D: IL-10 limits several inflammatory responses and can restrain antigen-presenting cells.
notes.E: IL-13 mediates type 2 effects such as mucus production rather than directing a Th1 programme.

questions.stem: Which cytokine most strongly promotes Th2-type differentiation and IgE class switching?
questions.why: IL-4 promotes the Th2 differentiation programme. In a B cell receiving appropriate additional signals such as CD40 stimulation, IL-4 also promotes switching towards IgE.

notes.A: IL-12 promotes Th1 differentiation and interferon-gamma responses rather than the characteristic IgE-promoting programme.
notes.B: Interferon-gamma is associated with Th1 responses and macrophage activation.
notes.D: IL-2 supports proliferation of activated T cells and maintenance of regulatory T cells, rather than instructing this IgE response.
notes.E: TNF contributes to inflammation and vascular activation rather than serving as the main Th2-polarising cytokine.

questions.stem: Which cytokine released by Th1 cells strongly activates macrophage antimicrobial function?
questions.why: Th1-derived interferon-gamma activates macrophages and increases their capacity to kill engulfed microbes. It is an important signal in immunity to intracellular infection.

notes.A: IL-4 is associated with type 2 responses and can induce a different macrophage activation programme.
notes.B: IL-5 principally supports eosinophil development, function and survival.
notes.C: IL-13 participates in type 2 responses and can favour alternative macrophage activation rather than classical antimicrobial activation.
notes.D: Transforming growth factor beta has regulatory and tissue-remodelling effects rather than being the hallmark Th1 activating signal here.

questions.stem: Which cytokine is strongly associated with eosinophil activation and survival?
questions.why: IL-5 promotes eosinophil differentiation and helps maintain survival and activity of mature eosinophils. It connects type 2 cytokine signalling to eosinophilic inflammation.

notes.A: IL-2 is a major cytokine supporting expansion and maintenance of T-cell populations.
notes.C: IL-12 is associated with Th1 and interferon-gamma responses rather than eosinophil survival.
notes.D: Interferon-alpha is a type I interferon with prominent antiviral effects.
notes.E: TNF promotes inflammation and endothelial activation, but IL-5 is more closely associated with eosinophil differentiation and survival.

questions.stem: In bacterial septic shock, which cytokine group is central to vascular inflammation and systemic effects?
questions.why: In bacterial sepsis, innate recognition can induce large amounts of TNF-alpha and IL-1. Together with other mediators, these cytokines contribute to fever, endothelial activation and vascular dysfunction.

notes.A: IL-4 and IL-13 are associated chiefly with type 2 responses rather than the classic early inflammatory signalling in septic shock.
notes.B: IL-5 supports eosinophils and eotaxin recruits them, which is characteristic of eosinophilic inflammation.
notes.C: IL-7 and IL-15 support lymphocyte development or maintenance rather than the acute vascular inflammatory response in the stem.
notes.E: IL-10 and TGF-beta can limit inflammation, although their roles in severe infection vary with timing and context.

questions.stem: Which immune messenger promotes clonal expansion of activated T lymphocytes?
questions.why: Activated T cells can produce IL-2 and upregulate its high-affinity receptor. IL-2 signalling promotes survival and cell-cycle progression, allowing responding clones to expand.

notes.B: IL-4 chiefly supports Th2 differentiation and certain B-cell class-switching responses rather than being the classic T-cell growth factor here.
notes.C: IL-5 is strongly associated with eosinophil development and survival.
notes.D: IL-13 mediates type 2 tissue responses such as mucus production rather than being the usual autocrine T-cell expansion signal.
notes.E: IL-18 supports interferon-gamma production in concert with other signals but is not the classic growth factor for activated T cells.
